rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.stem:
Two crystals \(\mathrm{C_1}\) and \(\mathrm{C_2}\), made of pure silicon, are doped with arsenic and aluminium respectively.
(i) Identify the extrinsic semiconductors so formed.
(ii) Why is doping of intrinsic semiconductors necessary ?
rows.solution:
**(i) Identifying the two.**

Silicon is tetravalent, so what matters is how many valence electrons the dopant brings.

| Crystal | Dopant | Valency | Semiconductor | Majority carriers |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| \(\mathrm{C_1}\) | Arsenic | 5 — pentavalent | **n-type** | electrons |
| \(\mathrm{C_2}\) | Aluminium | 3 — trivalent | **p-type** | holes |

In \(\mathrm{C_1}\), four of arsenic's five valence electrons complete the covalent bonds with neighbouring silicon atoms; the fifth is left over, bound so weakly that room temperature frees it. Arsenic is a **donor**.

In \(\mathrm{C_2}\), aluminium's three electrons leave one bond incomplete. That vacancy is a **hole**, and a neighbouring electron can move into it, so the hole travels. Aluminium is an **acceptor**.

**(ii) Why doping is necessary.**

A pure semiconductor is nearly useless as a circuit element, for two separate reasons.

**Its conductivity is far too low.** In intrinsic silicon the only carriers come from thermally broken covalent bonds, giving about \(10^{16}\) carriers per cubic metre against a metal's \(10^{29}\). Doping at roughly **one impurity atom in \(10^{6}\)** raises the carrier concentration by a factor of around \(10^{6}\), because the dopant level sits only \(\sim 0{\cdot}01\) eV from a band edge while the gap itself is \(1{\cdot}1\) eV.

**Its conductivity cannot be controlled.** In an intrinsic crystal \(n_e = n_h\) always, and the number is fixed by temperature alone — so the material's behaviour drifts with the weather and cannot be set by design. Doping makes the conductivity a **chosen** quantity: the dopant concentration sets it, and because the dopant is already fully ionised at room temperature the value stays nearly constant as the temperature changes.

The deeper reason, though, is the one the two crystals here are pointing at. **No useful device can be made from a single type of material.** A diode, a transistor, an LED and a solar cell are all built from a *junction* between p-type and n-type regions, and it is the junction — the depletion layer and its barrier potential — that does the work. Doping is what makes two distinguishable types exist at all.

rows.stem:
How will the interference pattern in Young's double-slit experiment be affected if :
(i) The screen is moved away from the plane of the slits.
(ii) The source slit is moved away from the plane of the slits.
(iii) The phase difference between the light waves emanating from the two slits \(\mathrm{S_1}\) and \(\mathrm{S_2}\) changes from 0 to \(\pi\) and remains constant.
rows.solution:
The fringe width in Young's experiment is

\(\beta = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d}\)

where \(D\) is the slit-to-screen distance and \(d\) the separation of the two slits. Notice what is *not* in it: the position of the **source** slit. That is what separates parts (i) and (ii).

**(i) The screen is moved away from the plane of the slits.**

\(D\) increases, and \(\beta \propto D\), so the **fringe width increases** — the whole pattern expands uniformly about the centre.

The fringes also become **fainter**, because the same light is spread over a larger area of screen. In practice this sets the limit on how far the screen can usefully be moved: past some distance the fringes are wide but too dim to see.

**(ii) The source slit is moved away from the plane of the slits.**

The **fringe width does not change at all** — \(\beta\) depends on \(\lambda\), \(D\) and \(d\), none of which has moved.

What changes is the **quality** of the pattern, and it improves. For fringes to be seen the two slits must be coherently illuminated, which requires

\(\dfrac{s}{S} < \dfrac{\lambda}{d}\)

where \(s\) is the size of the source slit and \(S\) its distance from the plane of the two slits. Increasing \(S\) makes the left-hand side smaller, so the condition is more comfortably satisfied and the fringes become **sharper and better defined**.

Against that, less light now reaches the slits, so the pattern is **dimmer**. Moving the source slit away therefore trades brightness for contrast.

(The reverse move is the destructive one: bring the source slit too close and \(s/S\) grows past \(\lambda/d\), different points of the source produce patterns displaced from one another, and the fringes wash out.)

**(iii) A constant phase difference of \(\pi\) is introduced between \(\mathrm{S_1}\) and \(\mathrm{S_2}\).**

The sources remain **coherent** — the phase difference is constant, which is all coherence requires — so a perfectly good interference pattern survives. The **fringe width is unchanged**.

What happens is that the whole pattern is **shifted by half a fringe**: maxima and minima swap places. At the centre of the screen the two paths are equal, so the geometric path difference is zero; but the waves now start \(\pi\) out of phase, so they arrive out of phase and cancel.

**The centre of the screen becomes dark**, where it was the brightest point before, and every bright fringe is replaced by a dark one.

This is worth distinguishing from the coherence failure in part (ii). There the pattern is *destroyed*; here it is merely *displaced*. A phase difference that stayed constant would be undetectable to anyone who did not know where the centre was — which is precisely why a *varying* phase difference, and not a large one, is what kills interference.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.stem:
An alpha particle is accelerated through a potential difference of 100 V. Calculate :
(i) The speed acquired by the alpha particle, and
(ii) The de-Broglie wavelength associated with it.
(Take mass of alpha particle \(= 6.4 \times 10^{-27}\) kg)
rows.solution:
**The data.** An alpha particle is a helium nucleus, so its charge is

\(q = 2e = 2 \times 1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19} = 3{\cdot}2 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}\)

with \(m = 6{\cdot}4 \times 10^{-27}\) kg and \(V = 100\) V.

**(i) The speed acquired.**

Accelerating through \(V\) converts electrical work into kinetic energy:

\(\tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} = qV \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2qV}{m}}\)

\(v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 3{\cdot}2 \times 10^{-19} \times 100}{6{\cdot}4 \times 10^{-27}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{6{\cdot}4 \times 10^{-17}}{6{\cdot}4 \times 10^{-27}}} = \sqrt{10^{10}}\)

\(v = 1 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)

The numbers are chosen to cancel exactly. At \(10^{5}\) m/s the particle is moving at about \(0{\cdot}03\%\) of the speed of light, so the non-relativistic formula is amply justified.

**(ii) The de Broglie wavelength.**

\(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{mv} = \dfrac{6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-34}}{6{\cdot}4 \times 10^{-27} \times 1 \times 10^{5}}\)

\(\lambda = \dfrac{6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-34}}{6{\cdot}4 \times 10^{-22}} \approx 1{\cdot}04 \times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m}\)

(The scheme rounds this to \(10^{-12}\) m.)

**How small that is.** About \(10^{-12}\) m is one hundredth of an atomic diameter — far shorter than the \(10^{-10}\) m spacing of atoms in a crystal, so an alpha particle at this energy will *not* show the diffraction that electrons of comparable energy do. The reason is mass: at the same accelerating voltage an electron acquires a wavelength of about \(1{\cdot}2\) Å, a hundred times longer, because \(\lambda = h/\sqrt{2mqV}\) and the electron is some \(7300\) times lighter.

That contrast is the practical content of the de Broglie relation: wave behaviour is not a property of small *energies* but of small **momenta**, and anything as massive as a nucleus hides its wave nature very effectively.

rows.subtopic: Bohr Model of the Hydrogen Atom
rows.stem:
(a) Use Bohr's postulate to prove that the radius of \(n^{th}\) orbit in a hydrogen atom is proportional to \(n^2\).
(b) How will the energy of a hydrogen atom change if \(n\) increases from 1 to \(\infty\) ?
rows.solution:
**(a) Proving \(r_n \propto n^{2}\).**

Two statements are needed, and only two.

**First — the dynamics.** The Coulomb attraction between the nucleus and the electron supplies the centripetal force for the circular orbit:

\(\dfrac{mv^{2}}{r} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{e^{2}}{r^{2}}\)

which rearranges to

\(mv^{2}r = \dfrac{e^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \qquad \ldots(1)\)

**Second — Bohr's quantization postulate.** Angular momentum is an integral multiple of \(h/2\pi\):

\(mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi} \qquad \ldots(2)\)

Now eliminate \(v\). Squaring (2) gives \(m^{2}v^{2}r^{2} = n^{2}h^{2}/4\pi^{2}\), and dividing that by (1):

\(\dfrac{m^{2}v^{2}r^{2}}{mv^{2}r} = \dfrac{n^{2}h^{2}/4\pi^{2}}{e^{2}/4\pi\varepsilon_0}\)

The left side collapses to \(mr\), so

\(r_n = \dfrac{n^{2}h^{2}\varepsilon_0}{\pi m e^{2}}\)

Every quantity on the right except \(n\) is a constant of nature, hence

\(r_n \propto n^{2}\)

Numerically \(r_1 = 0{\cdot}53\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}}\) — the Bohr radius — so \(r_2 = 2{\cdot}12\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}}\), \(r_3 = 4{\cdot}77\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}}\), and the orbits spread out rapidly.

**(b) The energy as \(n\) goes from 1 to \(\infty\).**

\(E_n = -\dfrac{13{\cdot}6}{n^{2}}\ \mathrm{eV}\)

\(n = 1: \quad E_1 = -13{\cdot}6\ \mathrm{eV} \qquad\qquad n \to \infty: \quad E_\infty = 0\)

**The energy increases**, from \(-13{\cdot}6\) eV up to zero — a rise of \(13{\cdot}6\) eV.

Three things are worth saying about that, because the negative signs mislead.

The energy is **rising** even though its magnitude is falling. It is negative throughout, and "less negative" means "greater".

The energy at \(n = \infty\) is **zero, not infinite**. Zero is the chosen reference: the electron at rest, infinitely far from the nucleus, free of it.

And the \(13{\cdot}6\) eV required to make that journey is exactly the **ionisation energy** of hydrogen from its ground state. Supplying it does not put the electron in a higher orbit; it removes the electron from the atom altogether.

The orbits also crowd together as they rise — the gap from \(n = 1\) to \(n = 2\) is \(10{\cdot}2\) eV while the whole of \(n = 4\) to \(\infty\) is only \(0{\cdot}85\) eV — because \(E_n\) goes as \(1/n^{2}\), just as \(r_n \propto n^{2}\) makes the orbits spread apart.
